'''winker-leather''' (wing′kėr-leᴛ̵ʜ″ėr), ''n.'' In ''saddlery'', a glazed piece of heavy leather which forms the outside of a winker or blind.

'''winker-muscle''' (wing′kėr-mus″l), ''n.'' Same as ''winker'', 5.

'''winker-plate''' (wing′kėr-plāt), ''n.'' In ''saddlery'', a metallic plate which gives shape and strength to a winker or blinder.

'''winker-strap''' (wing′kėr-strap), ''n.'' In ''saddlery'', a strap which holds the winkers in position. {{smaller|It extends downward from the crown-piece of the bridle, and then branches off on either side, and is fastened to the winkers. See cut under ''harness.''}}

'''winking''' (wing′king), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wynkkynge'', ''wynkynge;'' verbal n. of ''wink''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] The act of one who winks: often used in the colloquial phrase ''like winking''—that is, very rapidly; very quickly; with great vigor.

'''winkingly''' (wing′king-li), ''adv.'' With winking.

'''winkle<sup>1</sup>''' (wing′kl), ''n.'' [< AS. *''wincle'', in comp. ''pine-winclan'', periwinkles; allied to ''wink''<sup>1</sup>: see ''wink''<sup>2</sup> and ''periwinkle''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''periwinkle''<sup>2</sup>.

'''winkle<sup>2</sup>''' (wing′kl), ''a.'' A dialectal variant of ''wankle''. ''Halliwell.''

'''winkle-hawk''' (wing′kl-hâk), ''n.'' [D. ''winkelhaak'', a rent, tear.] An angular rent made in cloth, etc. ''Bartlett.'' Also ''winkle-hole''. [New York.]

'''winkless''' (wingk′les), ''a.'' [< ''wink''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less''.] Unwinking. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He advanced to that part of the area which was immediately below where I was standing, fixed on me a wide, dilated, ''winkless'' sort of stare, and halted.
{{right|''Proc. Soc. Psych. Research'', III. 94.}}}}

'''winly†''' (win′li), ''a.'' [ME., also ''wynnelich'', < AS. ''wynlīc'', joyous, < ''wyn'', joy (see ''winne''), + ''-līc'', E. ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''winsome''.] Joyous; winsome; pleasant; gracious; goodly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Chefly thay asken
Spycez, that vn-sparely men speded hom to bryng,
& the ''wynne-lych'' wyne ther-with.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 980.}}
<poem>That ''wynnelych'' lorde that wonyes in heuen.</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 1807.}}}}

'''winly''' (win′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''wynly'', ''wynli''; < ''winly'', ''a.''] '''1†.''' Delightfully; pleasantly.
{{smaller block|<poem>That was a perles place for ani prince of erthe,
& ''wynli'' with heie wal was closed al a-boute.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 749.}}
Thane I went to that wlonke, and ''wynly'' hire gretis.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3339.}}}}
'''2.''' Quietly. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''winna''' (win′ä). An assimilated form of ''wilna'', Scotch for ''will no''—that is, will not.

'''winnable''' (win′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''win''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able''.] Capable of being won.
{{smaller block|All the rest are ''winnable.''
{{right|''Pall Mall Gazette'', Feb. 18, 1888. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''winne†''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' Joy; delight; pleasure.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hit is min hiȝte [joy], hit is mi ''wune'',
That ich me draȝe to mine cunde [kind].</poem>
{{right|''Owl and Nightingale'', l. 272.}}
<poem>When I was borne Noye named he me,
And saide thees wordes with mekill ''wynne''.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 46.}}}}
'''II.''' ''a.'' Enjoyable; delightful.
{{smaller block|Ho wayned me vpon this wyse to your ''wynne'' halle.
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2456.}}}}

'''winnel, winnel-straw''' (win′el, -strâ), ''n.'' Same as ''jackstraw'', 5. [Prov. Eng.]

'''winner''' (win′ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wynner''; < ''win''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who or that which wins; a successful contestant or competitor.
{{smaller block|<poem>The event
Is yet to name the ''winner''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 5. 15.}}}}

'''winning''' (win′ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wynnynge'', ''wynynge''; verbal n. of ''win''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The act of one who wins, in any sense.
{{smaller block|At the ''Winning'' of Tonque [Towques], the King made eight and twenty Knights, and from thence marched with his Army to Caen.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 172.}}
If I am not worth the wooing, I surely am not worth the ''winning!''
{{right|''Longfellow'', Miles Standish, iii.}}}}

'''2.''' That which is won; that which is gained by effort, conquest, or successful competition; earnings; profit; gain: generally in the plural.
{{smaller block|The kynge Arthur made be leide on an hepe all the ''wyn-ynge'' and the richesse that ther was geten.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 167.}}
A . . . gamester, that stakes all his ''winnings'' upon every cast. {{right|''Addison'', Freeholder, No. 40.}}}}

'''3.''' In ''coal-mining'', a shaft or pit which is being sunk to win or open a bed of coal; an opening of any kind by which coal has been won; a bed of coal ready for mining (see ''win''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'', 9); sometimes, also, a part of a coal-mine, as distinguished from another portion from which it is separated by a barrier.
{{smaller block|The South Hetton and Great Hetton pits were also very costly difficult ''winnings'', on account of the quicksand and irruptions of water.
{{right|''Jevons'', The Coal Question (2d ed.), p. 68.}}}}

'''winning''' (win′ing), ''p. a.'' Successful in contending, competing, attaining, influencing, or gaining over; hence, especially, taking; attractive; charming.
{{smaller block|<poem>I do find
A ''winning'' language in your tongue and looks.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Custom of the Country, ii. 2.}}
<poem>Her smile, her speech, with ''winning'' sway,
Wiled the old harper’s mood away.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., ii. 10.}}}}

'''winning-headway''' (win′ing-hed″wā), ''n.'' In ''coal-mining'', a cross-heading, or one driven at right angles to the main gangways. [North. Eng.]

'''winningly''' (win′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a winning manner.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wink|6942|winnow}}</noinclude>''chan'', move aside, reel, nod, MHG. ''winken'' (pret. ''wank''), nod, also totter, reel, wince, G. ''winken'' (pret. ''winkte''), nod, make a sign, = Sw. ''vinka'', beckon, wink, = Dan. ''vinke'', beckon; cf. Icel. ''vanka'', wink, rove, = Sw. ''vanka'' = Dan. ''vanke'', rove, stroll; akin to AS. ''wancol'', wavering, E. ''wankle'', etc.: see ''wankle'', ''wench''<sup>1</sup>, ''wince''<sup>1</sup>, ''winch''<sup>2</sup>, etc.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To close and open the eyelids quickly; of the eyes, to be opened and shut quickly; blink; nictitate.
{{smaller block|Here is three studied, ere ye’ll thrice ''wink.''
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., i. 2. 54.}}}}
'''2.''' To shut the eyes; close the eyelids so as not to see.
{{smaller block|<poem>Unnethes wiste he how to loke or ''wynke.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 301.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A skilfull Gunner, with his left eye ''winking'',
Levels directly at an Oak hard by,
Whereon a hundred groaning Culuers cry.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 7.}}}}
'''3.''' To be wilfully blind or ignorant; avoid notice or recognition, as of an annoying or troublesome fact; ignore; connive: often followed by ''at.''
{{smaller block|<poem>If golde speake for her in the present tense,
The officer deputed for th’ offence
Will ''winck at'' smale faultes & remit correction.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 45.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You are forc’d to ''wink'' and seem content.</poem>
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Juvenal’s Eleventh Satire.}}}}
{{smaller block|We may surely ''wink at'' a few things for the sake of the public interest, if God Almighty does; and if He didn’t, I don’t know what would have become of the country.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, vii.}}}}

'''4†.''' To close the eyes in sleep; sleep.
{{smaller block|<poem>For wel I woot, although I wake or ''winke'',
Ye rekke not whether I flete or sinke.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Complaint to Pity, l. 109.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Go to bedde bi tyme, & ''wynke''.</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 50.}}}}

'''5.''' To convey a hint, wish, insinuation, etc., by a quick shutting and opening usually of one eye.
{{smaller block|<poem>Waryn Wisdome ''wynked'' vppon Mede,
And seide, “Madame, I am ȝowre man, what so my mouth Iangleth.”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), iv. 154.}}}}
{{smaller block|Pacience perceyued what I thouȝt, and ''wynked'' on me to be stille.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiii. 85.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Wink'' at the footman to leave him without a plate.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
{{smaller block|“Very well, sir,” cried the squire, who immediately smoked him, and ''winked'' on the rest of the company, to prepare us for the sport.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, vii.}}}}
{{smaller block|I blush to say I’ve ''winked'' at him, and he has ''winked'' at me!
{{right|''W. S. Gilbert'', Gentle Alice Brown.}}}}

'''6.''' To twinkle; shine with quick, irregular gleams; flash; sparkle.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whether the Heav’ns incessant agitation,
Into a Star transforming th’ Exhalation,
Kindle the same, like as a coal that ''winkt''
On a sticks end (and seemed quite extinct).</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And every Lamp, and every Fire,
Did at the dreadful Sight ''wink'' and expire.</poem>
{{right|''Cowley'', Pindaric Odes, xiv. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O for a beaker full of the warm South,
Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
With beaded bubbles ''winking'' at the brim.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Ode to a Nightingale.}}}}

{{smaller block|'''Winking muscle''', the sphincter or orbicular muscle of the eyelids, the action of which closes the eye; the winker: technically called ''palpebralis'' and ''orbicularis palpebrarum.'' See cut under ''muscle''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To close and open quickly: as, to ''wink'' the eyelids or the eyes.
{{smaller block|Lady Clavering, giving the young gentleman a delighted tap with her fan, ''winked'' her black eyes at him.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Pendennis, xxv.}}}}
'''2.''' To move, force, or remove by winking: as, to ''wink'' back one’s tears.

'''wink'''<sup>1</sup> (wingk), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wink'', sleep, = OHG. ''winch'', sideward movement, nod, MHG. ''winc'', ''wink'', G. ''wink'', nod; from the verb.]   '''1.''' A quick shutting and opening of the eyelids; especially, such a movement of one eye made as a signal; hence, a hint, insinuation, command, etc., conveyed by or as by winking.
{{smaller block|<poem>Eternall Father, at whose ''wink''
The wrathfull Ocean’s swelling pride doth sink.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|But why wou’d you ne’er give a Friend a ''Wink'' then?
{{right|''Wycherley'', Country Wife, v. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|In an instant my coachman took the ''wink'' to pursue.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 454.}}}}
'''2†.''' A nap; sleep.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thenne wakede I of my ''wink'', me was wo with alle
That I nedde [had not] sadloker i-slept.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), v. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' The time required for winking once; a very short space of time; a moment: referring usually to sleep.
{{smaller block|<poem>We never
Slept ''wink'' ashore all night, but made sail ever.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey, xvi. 491.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He’s harped them all asleep;
Except it was the king’s daughter
Who ae ''wink'' cou’dna get.</poem>
{{right|''The Water o’ Wearie’s Well'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 198).}}}}
{{smaller block|In a ''wink'' the false love turns to hate.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}}

'''4.''' A twinkle; a sparkle; a flash.
{{smaller block|<poem>A ''wink'' from Hesper falling
Fast in the wintry sky
Comes through the even blue,
Dear, like a word from you.</poem>
{{right|''W. E. Henley'', Echoes, xl.}}}}

'''Forty winks''', a short nap. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Old Mr. Transome, . . . since his walk, had been having ''forty winks'' on the sofa in the library.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xliii.}}}}

'''To tip one the wink.''' See ''tip''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wink'''<sup>2</sup> (wingk), ''n.''   [Short for ''winkle''<sup>1</sup>.]   A periwinkle. See ''periwinkle''<sup>2</sup>, and first quotation under ''wash'', ''n.'', 13. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|The ''wink'' men, as these periwinkle sellers are called, generally live in the lowest parts, and many in lodging-houses.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 78.}}}}

'''wink-a-peep''' (wingk′a̤-pēp), ''n.''   [As ''wink-and-peep''.]   The scarlet pimpernel, or shepherd’s weather-glass, ''Anagallis arvensis'': so named from its closing or winking in damp weather and opening or peeping in fair weather. By Bacon called ''wincopipe'' (which see).   ''Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''winker''' (wing′kėr), ''n.''   [< ''wink''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who winks.
{{smaller block|Nodders, ''winkers'', and whisperers. {{right|''Pope''.}}}}

'''2.''' One of the blinders of a horse; a blinker. —'''3.''' An eyelash; also, the eye. [Colloq.]—'''4.''' The nictitating or winking membrane of a bird’s eye; the third eyelid.—'''5.''' The winking muscle (which see, under ''wink''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'').—'''6.''' In an organ, a small bellows, compressed by a spring, attached to the side of a wind-trunk so as to regulate slight variations in the tension of the air within. Also called ''concussion-bellows.''

'''winningness''' (win′ing-nes), ''n.'' The property or character of being winning.
{{smaller block|Those who insist on charm, on ''winningness'' in style, on subtle harmonies and exquisite suggestion, are disappointed in Burke.

'''winning-post''' (win′ing-pōst), ''n.'' A post or goal in a race-course, the order of passing which determines the issue of the race.

'''winninish''' (win′in-ish), ''n.''   [Amer. Ind.]   The schoodic trout (which see, under ''trout''<sup>1</sup>).
{{smaller block|Found in Eastern waters under the name of “''winninish'',” “grayling,” “schoodic trout.”

'''winnow''' (win′ō), ''v.''   [< ME. ''winewen'', ''wynewen'', ''winwen'', ''windewen'', ''windwen'', ''wyndwe'', < AS. ''windwian'', ''wyndwian'', winnow, fan, ventilate (tr. L. ''ventilare''), with formative ''-w'', < ''wind'', wind, air: see ''wind''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'', and cf. ''wind''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'' Cf. Icel. ''vinza'', winnow, with formative ''-z'' (''-s''), < ''vindr'', wind (see ''winze''<sup>1</sup>), and L. ''ventilare'', ventilate, < ''ventus'', wind (see ''ventilate'').]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To fan; set in motion by means of wind; specifically, to expose (grain) to a current of air in order to separate and drive off chaff, refuse particles, etc.
